strings.b-00-meta.title: Units and Measurement
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.0: After this lesson you can explain what a unit, a base quantity and a derived unit are.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.1: After this lesson you can use significant figures, rounding and uncertainty rules in calculations.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.2: After this lesson you can write dimensional formulae and use dimensional analysis to check equations and deduce relations.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.0.definition: A standard reference with which a physical quantity is compared.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.1.definition: A fundamental quantity chosen for a system of units, such as length, mass and time.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.2.definition: A unit formed as a combination of base units for a derived quantity.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.3.definition: Reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit in a measurement.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.4.definition: Powers of base quantities that represent a physical quantity, written in square brackets.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.5.definition: Expression showing which base quantities represent the dimensions of a quantity.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.6.definition: The exponent b in a × 10b for an approximate estimate of a number.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.7.definition: Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added or subtracted.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.0: You measure length with a scale and mass with a balance. Measurement means comparison with a standard. That standard is called a unit.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.1: The result of measurement is a number with a unit. For example, a length is written as a number in metres.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.2: Units for base quantities are base units. Units for other quantities are derived units. All of them together form a system of units.
strings.b-02.question: What is the result of a measurement?
strings.b-02.options.1: A number accompanied by a unit
strings.b-02.explanation: Measurement compares a quantity with a unit, so the result is a number with a unit.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.0: Earlier systems were CGS, FPS and MKS. CGS used centimetre, gram and second. FPS used foot, pound and second. MKS used metre, kilogram and second.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.1: SI is now internationally accepted. It was developed by BIPM in 1971 and revised in November 2018. This book follows SI units.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.2: SI has seven base units. Plane angle has unit radian, rad. Solid angle has unit steradian, sr. Both are dimensionless. SI uses the decimal system.
strings.b-04.caption: Seven SI base quantities with their units and symbols.
strings.b-04.svg_texts.t-7: Seven SI base quantities and units
strings.b-05.question: Which set gives SI base units for length, mass and time?
strings.b-05.explanation: MKS and SI use metre, kilogram and second for length, mass and time.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.0: Significant figures are reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit. In 1.62 s, 1 and 6 are certain and 2 is uncertain, so there are three significant figures. In 287.5 cm there are four.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.1: All non-zero digits are significant. Zeros between two non-zero digits are significant. Zeros before the first non-zero digit in a number less than 1 are not significant.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.2: Trailing zeros without a decimal point are not significant. Trailing zeros with a decimal point are significant. Changing units does not change significant figures. Precision depends on the least count of the instrument.
strings.b-07.title: Scientific notation and order of magnitude
strings.b-07.steps.0.title: Write a × 10b
strings.b-07.steps.0.detail: Write the number as a × 10b where a is between 1 and 10 and b is any positive or negative exponent.
strings.b-07.steps.1.title: Find order of magnitude
strings.b-07.steps.1.detail: Round a to 1 for a ≤ 5 and to 10 for 5 < a ≤ 10. The number is then about 10b and b is the order of magnitude.
strings.b-07.steps.2.title: Use examples
strings.b-07.steps.2.detail: Earth diameter 1.28 × 107 m is of order 107 m with order 7. Hydrogen atom diameter 1.06 × 10-10 m is of order 10-10 m with order -10.
strings.b-07.steps.3.title: Trailing zeros
strings.b-07.steps.3.detail: In scientific notation all zeros in a are significant, so 4.700 m = 4.700 × 102 cm has four significant figures.
strings.b-08.question: How many significant figures are in 0.2370 g cm-3?
strings.b-08.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant and the trailing zero with a decimal point is significant, so 2, 3, 7 and 0 give four. Similarly 0.007 m2 has 1, 2.64 × 1024 kg has 3, 6.320 J has 4, 6.032 N m-2 has 4 and 0.0006032 m2 has 4.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.0: In multiplication or division, keep as many significant figures as the number with the least significant figures. Density 4.237 g divided by 2.51 cm3 is reported as 1.69 g cm-3, not to many decimal places.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.1: In addition or subtraction, keep as many decimal places as the number with the least decimal places. The sum 436.32 g, 227.2 g and 0.301 g is 663.8 g.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.2: The difference 0.307 m - 0.304 m is 0.003 m. Do not use the multiplication rule for addition and subtraction.
strings.b-10.problem: 5.74 g of a substance occupies 1.2 cm3. Express its density by keeping the significant figures in view.
strings.b-10.steps.0.title: Count significant figures
strings.b-10.steps.0.detail: Mass 5.74 g has 3 significant figures. Volume 1.2 cm3 has 2 significant figures.
strings.b-10.steps.1.title: Divide
strings.b-10.steps.2.title: Round to least
strings.b-10.steps.2.detail: Round to 2 significant figures, the least in the data.
strings.b-11.problem: Each side of a cube is measured to be 7.203 m. What are the total surface area and the volume of the cube to appropriate significant figures?
strings.b-11.steps.0.title: Count significant figures
strings.b-11.steps.0.detail: Length 7.203 m has 4 significant figures, so area and volume need 4.
strings.b-11.steps.1.title: Surface area
strings.b-11.steps.2.title: Volume
strings.b-12.title: Rounding off uncertain digits
strings.b-12.steps.0.title: Dropped digit more than 5
strings.b-12.steps.0.detail: Raise the preceding digit by 1. Example: 2.746 to three significant figures is 2.75.
strings.b-12.steps.1.title: Dropped digit less than 5
strings.b-12.steps.1.detail: Leave the preceding digit unchanged. Example: 1.743 to three significant figures is 1.74.
strings.b-12.steps.2.title: Dropped digit exactly 5
strings.b-12.steps.2.detail: If preceding digit is even, drop the 5. If odd, raise it by 1. So 2.745 becomes 2.74 and 2.735 becomes 2.74.
strings.b-12.steps.3.title: Intermediate steps
strings.b-12.steps.3.detail: Keep one extra digit in intermediate steps and round at the end to avoid building up rounding errors.
strings.b-13.question: 436.32 g + 227.2 g + 0.301 g = ? g to correct decimal places
strings.b-13.explanation: Arithmetic sum is 663.821 g, but 227.2 g is correct to only one decimal place, so round to 663.8 g.
strings.b-14.paragraphs.0: Uncertainty in a product combines. For a sheet 16.2 cm by 10.1 cm, each measurement is ± 0.1 cm, so area 163.62 cm2 has about 1.6% error and is quoted as 164 ± 3 cm2.
strings.b-14.paragraphs.1: Subtraction can reduce significant figures. 12.9 g - 7.06 g is 5.8 g, not 5.84 g, because decimal places matter.
strings.b-14.paragraphs.2: Relative error depends on the number itself. Keep one extra digit in intermediate steps of multi-step work.
strings.b-15.question: Both 1.02 g and 9.89 g are accurate to ± 0.01 g. Which has smaller relative error?
strings.b-15.explanation: Relative error in 1.02 g is (±0.01/1.02) × 100% = ±1%. In 9.89 g it is (±0.01/9.89) × 100% = ±0.1%, so 9.89 g has smaller relative error.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.0: Dimensions describe the nature of a quantity. Length is [L], mass is [M], time is [T], electric current is [A], temperature is [K], luminous intensity is [cd] and amount of substance is [mol].
strings.b-16.paragraphs.1: Volume is three lengths, so dimensions are [L3]. It has zero dimension in mass and time.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.2: Force is mass times acceleration, so dimensions are [M L T-2]. Magnitudes are not considered, so speed and velocity both have [L T-1].
strings.b-17.caption: Volume and force expressed in base dimensions.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.0: A dimensional formula shows how base quantities represent a quantity. Volume is [M0 L3 T0]. Speed is [M0 L T-1]. Acceleration is [M0 L T-2]. Mass density is [M L-3 T0].
strings.b-18.paragraphs.1: A dimensional equation equates a quantity with its formula. [V] = [M0 L3 T0], [v] = [M0 L T-1], [F] = [M L T-2] and [ρ] = [M L-3 T0].
strings.b-18.paragraphs.2: You get dimensional equations from relations between quantities by replacing each quantity with its dimensions.
strings.b-19.title: Checking x = x0 + v0 t + (1/2) a t2
strings.b-19.steps.0.title: Left side
strings.b-19.steps.1.title: First term right
strings.b-19.steps.2.title: Second term right
strings.b-19.steps.3.title: Third term right
strings.b-19.steps.4.title: Conclusion
strings.b-19.steps.4.detail: Each term has dimension of length, same as left side, so the equation is dimensionally correct. Passing does not prove it right.
strings.b-20.problem: Let us consider an equation 1/2 m v2 = m g h where m is the mass of the body, v its velocity, g is the acceleration due to gravity and h is the height. Check whether this equation is dimensionally correct.
strings.b-20.steps.0.title: Left side
strings.b-20.steps.1.title: Right side
strings.b-20.steps.2.title: Compare
strings.b-20.steps.2.detail: Dimensions of LHS and RHS are the same, so the equation is dimensionally correct.
strings.b-21.problem: The SI unit of energy is J = kg m2 s-2; that of speed v is m s-1 and of acceleration a is m s-2. Which of the formulae for kinetic energy (K) can you rule out on dimensional arguments (m stands for mass): (a) K = m2 v3 (b) K = (1/2) m v2 (c) K = m a (d) K = (3/16) m v2 (e) K = (1/2) m v2 + m a
strings.b-21.steps.0.title: Dimensions of K
strings.b-21.steps.0.detail: K has dimensions [M L2 T-2] from J = kg m2 s-2.
strings.b-21.steps.1.title: Check each formula
strings.b-21.steps.1.detail: (a) gives [M2 L3 T-3], (b) and (d) give [M L2 T-2], (c) gives [M L T-2], (e) adds quantities of different dimensions so has no proper dimensions.
strings.b-21.steps.2.title: Rule out
strings.b-21.steps.2.detail: (a), (c) and (e) are ruled out. Dimensions cannot distinguish (b) and (d). The correct formula is (b).
strings.b-21.answer: (a), (c) and (e) ruled out; correct is (b) K = (1/2) m v2
strings.b-22.title: Deducing pendulum period by dimensions
strings.b-22.steps.0.title: Assume product form
strings.b-22.steps.0.detail: Suppose period T depends on length l, mass m and gravity g as T = k lx gy mz, where k is dimensionless and x, y, z are exponents.
strings.b-22.steps.1.title: Match dimensions
strings.b-22.steps.1.detail: [T] = [L]x [L T-2]y [M]z gives Lx+y T-2y Mz, so x + y = 0, -2y = 1 and z = 0.
strings.b-22.steps.2.title: Solve
strings.b-22.steps.3.title: Constant
strings.b-22.steps.3.detail: k cannot be obtained by dimensions. Actually k = 2π, so T = 2π sqrt(l/g).
strings.b-23.title: Pendulum period versus length
strings.b-23.description: Shows period T = 2π sqrt(l/g) for a simple pendulum as length changes.
strings.b-23.controls.length.label: Length l (m)
strings.b-24.question: Which addition is allowed by the principle of homogeneity?
strings.b-24.explanation: Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added or subtracted. Length plus length has the same dimension [L] on both sides.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.0: Base quantities are length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity. Their units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.1: Derived units can have special names such as joule, newton and watt. Units in calculations are treated as algebraic quantities.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.2: Only proper significant figures should be retained. Dimensions check equations, but a dimensionally correct equation need not be exact and a dimensionally wrong equation must be wrong.
strings.b-26.problem: Fill in the blanks: (a) volume of a cube of side 1 cm in m3 (b) vehicle moving with speed 18 km h-1 covers m in 1 s (c) 1 kg m2 s-2 = g cm2 s-2 (d) 3.0 m s-2 = km h-2 (e) 1 m = ly (f) G = 6.67 × 10-11 N m2 (kg)-2 = (cm)3 s-2 g-1
strings.b-26.steps.0.title: Cube and vehicle
strings.b-26.steps.0.detail: 1 cm = 0.01 m, so volume = (0.01)3 = 1 × 10-6 m3. 18 km h-1 = 5 m s-1, so in 1 s it covers 5 m.
strings.b-26.steps.1.title: Energy unit
strings.b-26.steps.2.title: Acceleration
strings.b-26.steps.3.title: Light year and G
strings.b-26.steps.3.detail: Light year is 9.47 × 1015 m from the source example, so 1 m = 1.06 × 10-16 ly. For G, 1 N = 105 g cm s-2, giving 6.67 × 10-8 (cm)3 s-2 g-1.
strings.b-27.title: Calorie in new units
strings.b-27.steps.0.title: Start with calorie
strings.b-27.steps.0.detail: A calorie equals about 4.2 J and 1 J = 1 kg m2 s-2.
strings.b-27.steps.1.title: New units
strings.b-27.steps.1.detail: New unit of mass equals α kg, length equals β m and time equals γ s. Treat units as algebraic quantities.
strings.b-27.steps.2.title: Convert
strings.b-27.steps.2.detail: 1 kg = 1/α new mass units, 1 m = 1/β new length units, 1 s = 1/γ new time units, so 1 kg m2 s-2 = α-1 β-2 γ2 new units.
strings.b-27.steps.3.title: Result
strings.b-27.steps.3.detail: Calorie magnitude is 4.2 α-1 β-2 γ2 in the new units.
strings.b-28.question: Which statement is meaningful without specifying a standard for comparison?
strings.b-28.options.1: a jet plane moves with great speed
strings.b-28.options.2: a proton is much more massive than an electron
strings.b-28.options.3: the mass of Jupiter is very large
strings.b-28.explanation: Large or small is meaningless without a standard. Proton compared with electron specifies the standard, the electron, while the others do not specify a standard.
strings.b-29.question: A new unit of length is chosen so speed of light in vacuum is unity. Light takes 8 min and 20 s from Sun to Earth. What is the distance in the new unit?
strings.b-29.explanation: Time is 8 × 60 + 20 = 500 s. With speed = 1 in the new unit, distance = speed × time = 500 new units.
strings.b-30.question: Which is the most precise device for measuring length: (a) vernier callipers with 20 divisions on sliding scale (b) screw gauge of pitch 1 mm and 100 divisions on circular scale (c) optical instrument that can measure length to within a wavelength of light?
strings.b-30.explanation: Precision depends on least count. The optical instrument measures to within a wavelength of light, the smallest scale in the list, so it is the most precise.
strings.b-31.problem: A student measures the thickness of a human hair by looking at it through a microscope of magnification 100. He makes 20 observations and finds that the average width of the hair in the field of view of the microscope is 3.5 mm. What is the estimate on the thickness of hair?
strings.b-31.steps.0.title: Use magnification
strings.b-31.steps.0.detail: Actual thickness = observed width / magnification = 3.5 mm / 100.
strings.b-31.steps.1.title: Calculate
strings.b-31.steps.2.title: Significant figures
strings.b-31.steps.2.detail: 3.5 mm has 2 significant figures, so answer is 0.035 mm = 3.5 × 10-5 m.
strings.b-32.question: Why is a set of 100 measurements of the diameter of a thin brass rod expected to yield a more reliable estimate than a set of 5 measurements only?
strings.b-32.options.1: More observations give a more reliable average estimate
strings.b-32.explanation: More observations improve the average estimate. The same principle applies to estimating thread diameter with a metre scale and to repeated measurements in general.
strings.b-33.problem: The photograph of a house occupies an area of 1.75 cm2 on a 35 mm slide. The slide is projected on to a screen, and the area of the house on the screen is 1.55 m2. What is the linear magnification of the projector-screen arrangement?
strings.b-33.steps.0.title: Convert slide area
strings.b-33.steps.1.title: Area ratio
strings.b-33.steps.2.title: Linear magnification
strings.b-33.steps.2.detail: Linear magnification = sqrt(area ratio) = sqrt(8857) = 94.1 to three significant figures.
strings.b-34.problem: The length, breadth and thickness of a rectangular sheet of metal are 4.234 m, 1.005 m, and 2.01 cm respectively. Give the area and volume of the sheet to correct significant figures.
strings.b-34.steps.0.title: Area
strings.b-34.steps.0.detail: Area = 4.234 × 1.005 = 4.25517 m2. Both have 4 significant figures, so area = 4.255 m2.
strings.b-34.steps.1.title: Thickness in metres
strings.b-34.steps.2.title: Volume
strings.b-35.problem: The mass of a box measured by a grocer's balance is 2.30 kg. Two gold pieces of masses 20.15 g and 20.17 g are added to the box. What is (a) the total mass of the box, (b) the difference in the masses of the pieces to correct significant figures?
strings.b-35.steps.0.title: Total mass
strings.b-35.steps.0.detail: 2.30 kg = 2300 g correct to 10 g place. Total = 2300 + 20.15 + 20.17 = 2340.32 g, rounded by decimal places to 2340 g = 2.34 kg.
strings.b-35.steps.1.title: Difference
strings.b-35.steps.1.detail: Difference = 20.17 - 20.15 = 0.02 g, correct to two decimal places.
strings.b-36.question: A boy writes m/m0 = (1 - v2)-1/2 and forgets where to put c. Where must c go for dimensional correctness?
strings.b-36.options.0: With v as v/c inside the bracket
strings.b-36.explanation: v and c both have dimensions [L T-1], so v/c is dimensionless. The argument of the function must be dimensionless, and ratio of similar quantities is dimensionless.
strings.b-37.problem: The unit of length convenient on the atomic scale is known as an angstrom and is denoted by Å: 1 Å = 10-10 m. The size of a hydrogen atom is about 0.5 Å. What is the total atomic volume in m3 of a mole of hydrogen atoms?
strings.b-37.steps.0.title: Volume per atom
strings.b-37.steps.1.title: Number per mole
strings.b-37.steps.1.detail: One mole contains 6.02214076 × 1023 elementary entities from the mole definition.
strings.b-37.steps.2.title: Total volume
strings.b-38.question: One mole of an ideal gas at standard temperature and pressure occupies 22.4 L. Taking size of hydrogen molecule as about 1 Å, what is the ratio of molar volume to atomic volume of a mole of hydrogen?
strings.b-38.explanation: Molar volume = 22.4 L = 2.24 × 10-2 m3. Atomic volume = (1 × 10-10)3 × 6.022 × 1023 = 6.0 × 10-7 m3. Ratio = 2.24 × 10-2 / 6.0 × 10-7 = 3.7 × 104. The ratio is large because in a gas atoms are far apart and most of the volume is empty space between them.
strings.b-39.question: If you look out of a fast moving train, nearby trees seem to move rapidly opposite to the train but distant objects seem stationary. Why?
strings.b-39.options.0: Nearby objects move faster than the train
strings.b-39.options.1: Nearby objects change direction quickly relative to you, distant objects change direction very slowly
strings.b-39.options.2: Distant objects are stationary in space
strings.b-39.options.3: Light from distant objects is slower
strings.b-39.explanation: Apparent motion depends on how fast the direction to the object changes for the moving observer. Nearby objects change direction quickly, distant objects change direction slowly, so they seem to move with you or be stationary.
strings.b-40.problem: The Sun is a hot plasma with inner core temperature exceeding 107 K and outer surface about 6000 K. Expect the mass density of the Sun to be in the range of solids and liquids or gases? Check with mass of the Sun = 2.0 × 1030 kg, radius of the Sun = 7.0 × 108 m.
strings.b-40.steps.0.title: Volume of Sun
strings.b-40.steps.1.title: Density
strings.b-40.steps.2.title: Compare range
strings.b-40.steps.2.detail: 1.4 × 103 kg m-3 is in the range of solids and liquids, not gases, so the guess for solids and liquids range is correct.
strings.b-40.answer: 1.4 × 103 kg m-3, in the range of solids and liquids
strings.b-41.question: What does dimensional analysis tell us about an equation?
strings.b-41.options.0: A dimensionally correct equation must be exact
strings.b-41.options.1: A dimensionally correct equation need not be exact, but a dimensionally wrong equation must be wrong
strings.b-41.options.3: Dimensions can distinguish quantities with same dimensions
strings.b-41.explanation: If an equation fails the test it is proved wrong. If it passes, it is not proved right. Constants cannot be obtained and quantities with same dimensions cannot be distinguished.

lesson.title: Units and Measurement
objectives: After this lesson you can explain what a unit, a base quantity and a derived unit are.
After this lesson you can use significant figures, rounding and uncertainty rules in calculations.
After this lesson you can write dimensional formulae and use dimensional analysis to check equations and deduce relations.

sections.title: Introduction: What is measurement?
paragraphs: You measure things every day. You use a scale for length. You use a balance for mass. You use a clock for time.
Measurement means comparison. You compare a quantity with a standard. That standard is called a unit.
The result is a number with a unit. For example, 5 m means 5 times the unit metre.
Some quantities are basic. They are called base quantities. Their units are base units.
Other quantities are made from base quantities. Their units are derived units. All base and derived units together form a system of units.

sections.title: The International System of Units
paragraphs: Earlier, different countries used different systems. CGS used centimetre, gram and second. FPS used foot, pound and second. MKS used metre, kilogram and second.
Now the world uses SI. SI means Système International d'Unités. It is the International System of Units.
SI has seven base units. They are for length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.
Their units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Their symbols are m, kg, s, A, K, mol and cd.
Plane angle has unit radian, symbol rad. Solid angle has unit steradian, symbol sr. Both are dimensionless. SI uses the decimal system, so conversions are simple.

sections.title: Significant figures
paragraphs: Every measurement has error. So you must show precision. Significant figures show precision.
Significant figures are reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit. In 1.62 s, 1 and 6 are certain and 2 is uncertain. So there are three significant figures.
All non-zero digits are significant. Zeros between two non-zero digits are significant. Zeros before the first non-zero digit in a number less than 1 are not significant.
Trailing zeros without a decimal point are not significant. Trailing zeros with a decimal point are significant. Changing units does not change significant figures.
Scientific notation is the best way to show this. Write a number as a × 10b, where a is between 1 and 10. The exponent b is the order of magnitude.

sections.title: Arithmetic, rounding and uncertainty
paragraphs: In multiplication or division, keep as many significant figures as the number with the least significant figures. In addition or subtraction, keep as many decimal places as the number with the least decimal places.
Rounding means dropping extra uncertain digits. If the dropped digit is more than 5, raise the preceding digit by 1. If it is less than 5, leave it unchanged.
If the dropped digit is exactly 5, look at the preceding digit. If it is even, drop the 5. If it is odd, raise it by 1.
In multi-step work, keep one extra digit in intermediate steps. Round only at the end. This stops rounding errors from building up.
Uncertainty can be shown as plus or minus. Relative error depends on the number itself, not only on significant figures.

sections.title: Dimensions of physical quantities
paragraphs: Dimensions describe the nature of a quantity. We write dimensions in square brackets. Length is [L], mass is [M] and time is [T].
Electric current is [A], temperature is [K], luminous intensity is [cd] and amount of substance is [mol].
Volume is length times length times length. So its dimensions are [L3]. It has zero dimension in mass and time.
Force is mass times acceleration. Acceleration is length divided by time squared. So force has dimensions [M L T-2].
Magnitudes are not considered here. Only the type of quantity matters. Speed and velocity both have dimensions [L T-1].

sections.title: Dimensional formulae and equations
paragraphs: A dimensional formula shows how base quantities represent a quantity. Volume has formula [M0 L3 T0]. Speed has formula [M0 L T-1].
Acceleration has formula [M0 L T-2]. Mass density has formula [M L-3 T0]. The zero means that base quantity is absent.
A dimensional equation equates a quantity with its formula. For example, [V] = [M0 L3 T0] and [F] = [M L T-2].
You can get a dimensional equation from a relation between quantities. You replace each quantity by its dimensions.

sections.title: Dimensional analysis and its applications
paragraphs: Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added or subtracted. This is the principle of homogeneity of dimensions. It helps you check an equation.
If dimensions on both sides do not match, the equation is wrong. If they match, the equation may still be wrong. Passing the test does not prove it right.
Dimensional analysis can also deduce a relation. You assume the quantity depends on other quantities as a product. Then you match dimensions on both sides.
This method cannot give dimensionless constants. It also cannot distinguish quantities with the same dimensions.

sections.title: Summary
paragraphs: Physics is based on measurement of physical quantities. Base quantities are chosen first. Their units are base units.
Derived quantities are combinations of base quantities. Their units are derived units. SI is the international system with seven base units.
Measurements should be written in scientific notation when needed. Only proper significant figures should be retained.
Dimensions describe the nature of quantities. Dimensional analysis checks equations and deduces relations. A dimensionally wrong equation must be wrong.

glossary.definition: A standard reference with which a physical quantity is compared.
A fundamental quantity chosen for a system of units, such as length, mass and time.
A unit formed as a combination of base units for a derived quantity.
Reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit in a measurement.
Powers of base quantities that represent a physical quantity, written in square brackets.
Expression showing which base quantities represent the dimensions of a quantity.
The exponent b in a × 10b for an approximate estimate of a number.
Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added or subtracted.

paragraphs: You measure length with a scale and mass with a balance. Measurement means comparison with a standard. That standard is called a unit.
The result of measurement is a number with a unit. For example, a length is written as a number in metres.
Units for base quantities are base units. Units for other quantities are derived units. All of them together form a system of units.

spec.question: What is the result of a measurement?
options: A number accompanied by a unit
spec.explanation: Measurement compares a quantity with a unit, so the result is a number with a unit.
spec.expected_understanding: Student knows measurement is comparison with a unit and is reported as number plus unit.

paragraphs: Earlier systems were CGS, FPS and MKS. CGS used centimetre, gram and second. FPS used foot, pound and second. MKS used metre, kilogram and second.
SI is now internationally accepted. It was developed by BIPM in 1971 and revised in November 2018. This book follows SI units.
SI has seven base units. Plane angle has unit radian, rad. Solid angle has unit steradian, sr. Both are dimensionless. SI uses the decimal system.

spec.question: Which set gives SI base units for length, mass and time?
spec.explanation: MKS and SI use metre, kilogram and second for length, mass and time.
spec.expected_understanding: Student can identify SI base units and distinguish CGS, FPS and MKS.

paragraphs: Significant figures are reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit. In 1.62 s, 1 and 6 are certain and 2 is uncertain, so there are three significant figures. In 287.5 cm there are four.
All non-zero digits are significant. Zeros between two non-zero digits are significant. Zeros before the first non-zero digit in a number less than 1 are not significant.

Trailing zeros without a decimal point are not significant. Trailing zeros with a decimal point are significant. Changing units does not change significant figures. Precision depends on the least count of the instrument.

spec.title: Scientific notation and order of magnitude

steps.title: Write a × 10b
steps.detail: Write the number as a × 10b where a is between 1 and 10 and b is any positive or negative exponent.

steps.title: Find order of magnitude
steps.detail: Round a to 1 for a ≤ 5 and to 10 for 5 < a ≤ 10. The number is then about 10b and b is the order of magnitude.

steps.title: Use examples
steps.detail: Earth diameter 1.28 × 107 m is of order 107 m with order 7. Hydrogen atom diameter 1.06 × 10-10 m is of order 10-10 m with order -10.

steps.title: Trailing zeros
steps.detail: In scientific notation all zeros in a are significant, so 4.700 m = 4.700 × 102 cm has four significant figures.

spec.question: How many significant figures are in 0.2370 g cm-3?
spec.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant and the trailing zero with a decimal point is significant, so 2, 3, 7 and 0 give four. Similarly 0.007 m2 has 1, 2.64 × 1024 kg has 3, 6.320 J has 4, 6.032 N m-2 has 4 and 0.0006032 m2 has 4.
spec.expected_understanding: Student applies significant figure rules to numbers less than 1 and with trailing zeros.

paragraphs: In multiplication or division, keep as many significant figures as the number with the least significant figures. Density 4.237 g divided by 2.51 cm3 is reported as 1.69 g cm-3, not to many decimal places.
In addition or subtraction, keep as many decimal places as the number with the least decimal places. The sum 436.32 g, 227.2 g and 0.301 g is 663.8 g.
The difference 0.307 m - 0.304 m is 0.003 m. Do not use the multiplication rule for addition and subtraction.

spec.problem: 5.74 g of a substance occupies 1.2 cm3. Express its density by keeping the significant figures in view.

steps.title: Count significant figures
steps.detail: Mass 5.74 g has 3 significant figures. Volume 1.2 cm3 has 2 significant figures.

steps.title: Round to least
steps.detail: Round to 2 significant figures, the least in the data.

spec.problem: Each side of a cube is measured to be 7.203 m. What are the total surface area and the volume of the cube to appropriate significant figures?

steps.title: Count significant figures
steps.detail: Length 7.203 m has 4 significant figures, so area and volume need 4.

steps.title: Dropped digit more than 5
steps.detail: Raise the preceding digit by 1. Example: 2.746 to three significant figures is 2.75.

steps.title: Dropped digit less than 5
steps.detail: Leave the preceding digit unchanged. Example: 1.743 to three significant figures is 1.74.

steps.title: Dropped digit exactly 5
steps.detail: If preceding digit is even, drop the 5. If odd, raise it by 1. So 2.745 becomes 2.74 and 2.735 becomes 2.74.

steps.title: Intermediate steps
steps.detail: Keep one extra digit in intermediate steps and round at the end to avoid building up rounding errors.

spec.question: 436.32 g + 227.2 g + 0.301 g = ? g to correct decimal places
spec.explanation: Arithmetic sum is 663.821 g, but 227.2 g is correct to only one decimal place, so round to 663.8 g.
spec.expected_understanding: Student uses decimal places rule for addition, not significant figures.

paragraphs: Uncertainty in a product combines. For a sheet 16.2 cm by 10.1 cm, each measurement is ± 0.1 cm, so area 163.62 cm2 has about 1.6% error and is quoted as 164 ± 3 cm2.
Subtraction can reduce significant figures. 12.9 g - 7.06 g is 5.8 g, not 5.84 g, because decimal places matter.
Relative error depends on the number itself. Keep one extra digit in intermediate steps of multi-step work.

spec.question: Both 1.02 g and 9.89 g are accurate to ± 0.01 g. Which has smaller relative error?
spec.explanation: Relative error in 1.02 g is (±0.01/1.02) × 100% = ±1%. In 9.89 g it is (±0.01/9.89) × 100% = ±0.1%, so 9.89 g has smaller relative error.
spec.expected_understanding: Student calculates relative error and sees it depends on the number itself.

paragraphs: Dimensions describe the nature of a quantity. Length is [L], mass is [M], time is [T], electric current is [A], temperature is [K], luminous intensity is [cd] and amount of substance is [mol].
Volume is three lengths, so dimensions are [L3]. It has zero dimension in mass and time.
Force is mass times acceleration, so dimensions are [M L T-2]. Magnitudes are not considered, so speed and velocity both have [L T-1].

paragraphs: A dimensional formula shows how base quantities represent a quantity. Volume is [M0 L3 T0]. Speed is [M0 L T-1]. Acceleration is [M0 L T-2]. Mass density is [M L-3 T0].
A dimensional equation equates a quantity with its formula. [V] = [M0 L3 T0], [v] = [M0 L T-1], [F] = [M L T-2] and [ρ] = [M L-3 T0].
You get dimensional equations from relations between quantities by replacing each quantity with its dimensions.

spec.title: Checking x = x0 + v0 t + (1/2) a t2

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.detail: Each term has dimension of length, same as left side, so the equation is dimensionally correct. Passing does not prove it right.

spec.problem: Let us consider an equation 1/2 m v2 = m g h where m is the mass of the body, v its velocity, g is the acceleration due to gravity and h is the height. Check whether this equation is dimensionally correct.

steps.title: Compare
steps.detail: Dimensions of LHS and RHS are the same, so the equation is dimensionally correct.

spec.problem: The SI unit of energy is J = kg m2 s-2; that of speed v is m s-1 and of acceleration a is m s-2. Which of the formulae for kinetic energy (K) can you rule out on dimensional arguments (m stands for mass): (a) K = m2 v3 (b) K = (1/2) m v2 (c) K = m a (d) K = (3/16) m v2 (e) K = (1/2) m v2 + m a

steps.title: Dimensions of K
steps.detail: K has dimensions [M L2 T-2] from J = kg m2 s-2.

steps.title: Check each formula
steps.detail: (a) gives [M2 L3 T-3], (b) and (d) give [M L2 T-2], (c) gives [M L T-2], (e) adds quantities of different dimensions so has no proper dimensions.

steps.title: Rule out
steps.detail: (a), (c) and (e) are ruled out. Dimensions cannot distinguish (b) and (d). The correct formula is (b).

spec.answer: (a), (c) and (e) ruled out; correct is (b) K = (1/2) m v2

steps.title: Assume product form
steps.detail: Suppose period T depends on length l, mass m and gravity g as T = k lx gy mz, where k is dimensionless and x, y, z are exponents.

steps.title: Match dimensions
steps.detail: [T] = [L]x [L T-2]y [M]z gives Lx+y T-2y Mz, so x + y = 0, -2y = 1 and z = 0.

steps.title: Constant
steps.detail: k cannot be obtained by dimensions. Actually k = 2π, so T = 2π sqrt(l/g).

spec.title: Pendulum period versus length
spec.description: Shows period T = 2π sqrt(l/g) for a simple pendulum as length changes.
spec.learning_goal: See how period increases with length and that mass does not appear in the dimensional result.
spec.default_behaviour: Shows the period for l = 1 m computed from T = 2π sqrt(l/g) with g = 9.8 m s-2.

spec.question: Which addition is allowed by the principle of homogeneity?
spec.explanation: Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added or subtracted. Length plus length has the same dimension [L] on both sides.
spec.expected_understanding: Student applies homogeneity principle to addition and subtraction.

paragraphs: Base quantities are length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity. Their units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
Derived units can have special names such as joule, newton and watt. Units in calculations are treated as algebraic quantities.
Only proper significant figures should be retained. Dimensions check equations, but a dimensionally correct equation need not be exact and a dimensionally wrong equation must be wrong.

spec.problem: Fill in the blanks: (a) volume of a cube of side 1 cm in m3 (b) vehicle moving with speed 18 km h-1 covers m in 1 s (c) 1 kg m2 s-2 = g cm2 s-2 (d) 3.0 m s-2 = km h-2 (e) 1 m = ly (f) G = 6.67 × 10-11 N m2 (kg)-2 = (cm)3 s-2 g-1

steps.title: Cube and vehicle
steps.detail: 1 cm = 0.01 m, so volume = (0.01)3 = 1 × 10-6 m3. 18 km h-1 = 5 m s-1, so in 1 s it covers 5 m.

steps.title: Light year and G
steps.detail: Light year is 9.47 × 1015 m from the source example, so 1 m = 1.06 × 10-16 ly. For G, 1 N = 105 g cm s-2, giving 6.67 × 10-8 (cm)3 s-2 g-1.

steps.title: Start with calorie
steps.detail: A calorie equals about 4.2 J and 1 J = 1 kg m2 s-2.

steps.title: New units
steps.detail: New unit of mass equals α kg, length equals β m and time equals γ s. Treat units as algebraic quantities.

steps.title: Convert
steps.detail: 1 kg = 1/α new mass units, 1 m = 1/β new length units, 1 s = 1/γ new time units, so 1 kg m2 s-2 = α-1 β-2 γ2 new units.

steps.title: Result
steps.detail: Calorie magnitude is 4.2 α-1 β-2 γ2 in the new units.

spec.question: Which statement is meaningful without specifying a standard for comparison?
options: a jet plane moves with great speed
a proton is much more massive than an electron
the mass of Jupiter is very large
spec.explanation: Large or small is meaningless without a standard. Proton compared with electron specifies the standard, the electron, while the others do not specify a standard.
spec.expected_understanding: Student understands large and small need a standard for comparison.

spec.question: A new unit of length is chosen so speed of light in vacuum is unity. Light takes 8 min and 20 s from Sun to Earth. What is the distance in the new unit?
spec.explanation: Time is 8 × 60 + 20 = 500 s. With speed = 1 in the new unit, distance = speed × time = 500 new units.
spec.expected_understanding: Student uses distance = speed × time with the new unit definition.

spec.question: Which is the most precise device for measuring length: (a) vernier callipers with 20 divisions on sliding scale (b) screw gauge of pitch 1 mm and 100 divisions on circular scale (c) optical instrument that can measure length to within a wavelength of light?
spec.explanation: Precision depends on least count. The optical instrument measures to within a wavelength of light, the smallest scale in the list, so it is the most precise.
spec.expected_understanding: Student compares precision by least count principle.

spec.problem: A student measures the thickness of a human hair by looking at it through a microscope of magnification 100. He makes 20 observations and finds that the average width of the hair in the field of view of the microscope is 3.5 mm. What is the estimate on the thickness of hair?

steps.title: Use magnification
steps.detail: Actual thickness = observed width / magnification = 3.5 mm / 100.

steps.title: Significant figures
steps.detail: 3.5 mm has 2 significant figures, so answer is 0.035 mm = 3.5 × 10-5 m.

spec.question: Why is a set of 100 measurements of the diameter of a thin brass rod expected to yield a more reliable estimate than a set of 5 measurements only?
options: More observations give a more reliable average estimate
spec.explanation: More observations improve the average estimate. The same principle applies to estimating thread diameter with a metre scale and to repeated measurements in general.
spec.expected_understanding: Student understands repeated measurements improve reliability.

spec.problem: The photograph of a house occupies an area of 1.75 cm2 on a 35 mm slide. The slide is projected on to a screen, and the area of the house on the screen is 1.55 m2. What is the linear magnification of the projector-screen arrangement?

steps.title: Linear magnification
steps.detail: Linear magnification = sqrt(area ratio) = sqrt(8857) = 94.1 to three significant figures.

spec.problem: The length, breadth and thickness of a rectangular sheet of metal are 4.234 m, 1.005 m, and 2.01 cm respectively. Give the area and volume of the sheet to correct significant figures.

steps.title: Area
steps.detail: Area = 4.234 × 1.005 = 4.25517 m2. Both have 4 significant figures, so area = 4.255 m2.

steps.title: Thickness in metres
steps.detail: 2.01 cm = 0.0201 m, with 3 significant figures.

steps.title: Volume
steps.detail: Volume = 4.255 × 0.0201 = 0.0855 m3 to 3 significant figures.

spec.problem: The mass of a box measured by a grocer's balance is 2.30 kg. Two gold pieces of masses 20.15 g and 20.17 g are added to the box. What is (a) the total mass of the box, (b) the difference in the masses of the pieces to correct significant figures?

steps.title: Total mass
steps.detail: 2.30 kg = 2300 g correct to 10 g place. Total = 2300 + 20.15 + 20.17 = 2340.32 g, rounded by decimal places to 2340 g = 2.34 kg.

steps.title: Difference
steps.detail: Difference = 20.17 - 20.15 = 0.02 g, correct to two decimal places.

spec.question: A boy writes m/m0 = (1 - v2)-1/2 and forgets where to put c. Where must c go for dimensional correctness?
options: With v as v/c inside the bracket
spec.explanation: v and c both have dimensions [L T-1], so v/c is dimensionless. The argument of the function must be dimensionless, and ratio of similar quantities is dimensionless.
spec.expected_understanding: Student places c with v to make a dimensionless ratio.

spec.problem: The unit of length convenient on the atomic scale is known as an angstrom and is denoted by Å: 1 Å = 10-10 m. The size of a hydrogen atom is about 0.5 Å. What is the total atomic volume in m3 of a mole of hydrogen atoms?

steps.title: Number per mole
steps.detail: One mole contains 6.02214076 × 1023 elementary entities from the mole definition.

spec.question: One mole of an ideal gas at standard temperature and pressure occupies 22.4 L. Taking size of hydrogen molecule as about 1 Å, what is the ratio of molar volume to atomic volume of a mole of hydrogen?
spec.explanation: Molar volume = 22.4 L = 2.24 × 10-2 m3. Atomic volume = (1 × 10-10)3 × 6.022 × 1023 = 6.0 × 10-7 m3. Ratio = 2.24 × 10-2 / 6.0 × 10-7 = 3.7 × 104. The ratio is large because in a gas atoms are far apart and most of the volume is empty space between them.
spec.expected_understanding: Student computes molar to atomic volume ratio and explains why it is large.

spec.question: If you look out of a fast moving train, nearby trees seem to move rapidly opposite to the train but distant objects seem stationary. Why?
options: Nearby objects move faster than the train
Nearby objects change direction quickly relative to you, distant objects change direction very slowly
Distant objects are stationary in space
Light from distant objects is slower
spec.explanation: Apparent motion depends on how fast the direction to the object changes for the moving observer. Nearby objects change direction quickly, distant objects change direction slowly, so they seem to move with you or be stationary.
spec.expected_understanding: Student explains apparent motion by relative change of direction.

spec.problem: The Sun is a hot plasma with inner core temperature exceeding 107 K and outer surface about 6000 K. Expect the mass density of the Sun to be in the range of solids and liquids or gases? Check with mass of the Sun = 2.0 × 1030 kg, radius of the Sun = 7.0 × 108 m.

steps.title: Compare range
steps.detail: 1.4 × 103 kg m-3 is in the range of solids and liquids, not gases, so the guess for solids and liquids range is correct.

spec.answer: 1.4 × 103 kg m-3, in the range of solids and liquids

spec.question: What does dimensional analysis tell us about an equation?
options: A dimensionally correct equation must be exact
A dimensionally correct equation need not be exact, but a dimensionally wrong equation must be wrong
Dimensions can distinguish quantities with same dimensions
spec.explanation: If an equation fails the test it is proved wrong. If it passes, it is not proved right. Constants cannot be obtained and quantities with same dimensions cannot be distinguished.
spec.expected_understanding: Student states the limits of dimensional analysis correctly.
